[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to keep this focused on runtime profiling and concrete next steps. Nina from engineering will drive.
[00:18] Nina (SE): Hi all, Nina here. Quick agenda: kernel selection and op fusion, CUDA graph warmup, KV cache hit ratios and placement, batching heuristics, and quantization tradeoffs. We'll look for what matters to KiteAnalytics' 8B model and your 50ms per-request SLO.
[00:32] Raj (Infra Eng): Thanks, yeah 50ms is the ballpark for our interactive endpoint with 2k context, but we are open to slightly higher p95 during peak if throughput grows. Also we have on-prem racks with A100s connected via NVLINK in a VPC-like setup.
[00:48] Nina (SE): Great. Can you confirm the model family? Is it a Llama-2-8B derivative or something custom?
[00:55] Maya (ML Eng): It's a slightly distilled Llama-2-8B variant with a few custom tokenizers and some fused attention modules. Huggingface format, weights only.
[01:05] Jonas (SRE): Quick infra note: we prefer local KV cache stored in shared memory across processes rather than hitting a remote cache to keep latency predictable.
[01:12] Nina (SE): That's an important constraint. Local KV cache improves latency but complicates multi-tenant memory isolation. We'll talk tradeoffs.
[01:20] Alex (AE): Also mention security constraints — VPC, KMS, and SOC2 logs — for the on-prem pilot. Caroline, anything to add?
[01:27] Caroline (CTO): We need auditability; any local cache must have access logs. Also encryption at rest for model weights is a must.
[01:34] Nina (SE): Understood — Redwood Private supports KMS for keys and we can add audit hooks. For the runtime specifics, I'll jump into profiling notes.

--- Profiling and kernel selection ---
[01:50] Nina (SE): First, kernel selection: TensorRT-LLM aggressively fuses attention and FFN ops into fewer kernels, which reduces kernel launch overhead but can increase memory working set. vLLM leans on smaller primitives and more CPU scheduling for batching, which can be beneficial when KV cache hits are high. We've seen different behavior depending on sequence length and batch shape.
[02:17] Maya (ML Eng): Can you quantify? For 2k context and 8-token generation, what's typical latency delta?
[02:25] Nina (SE): In our internal runs with an 8B model, TensorRT-LLM compiled engines gave ~20-35% lower per-token latency at mid-range throughput when batch sizes hit 4-8, but required a longer compile/warmup and more VRAM. vLLM had slightly higher single-request latency but excelled at tiny-batch scenarios due to its continuous batching and fast KV lookup.
[02:52] Raj (Infra Eng): So when KV cache hit ratio is high, vLLM might win?
[02:58] Nina (SE): Right — because vLLM's path for cache hits avoids recomputing large attention matmuls; it's very efficient at serving recurrent tokens. TensorRT-LLM's fused kernels still execute, though faster per-op, so the crossover depends on context length and how many tokens are reused.

--- CUDA graphs and warmup ---
[03:20] Nina (SE): CUDA graphs: TensorRT-LLM benefits a lot from CUDA graph capture for fixed-length, stable workloads. But the cost: first capture can take 100-300ms and must be repeated per sequence length and batch shape. If you have many variable prompt lengths, graph proliferation hurts.
[03:43] Jonas (SRE): We saw graph capture stutter in a previous stack — it caused 200ms tails during the first requests of new shapes. Any mitigations?
[03:51] Nina (SE): Two: pre-warm all expected shapes at startup using representative leaky inputs; or use a lightweight dynamic graph fallback. Also Redwood runtime supports graph cache eviction and reuse policies. We'll share our graph warmup scripts.
[04:06] Raj (Infra Eng): Do you have numbers for the capture overhead on A100 vs H100?
[04:10] Nina (SE): A100 typical capture ~150-250ms depending on engine complexity; H100 can be faster but depends on driver and cuBLAS/cuDNN versions. We'll include driver matrix in artifacts.

--- KV cache placement and consistency ---
[04:28] Nina (SE): On KV cache, there are three patterns: local process-shared RAM, node-local SSD-backed (less common), and remote KV over RDMA/redis-like. For low tail latency we prefer process-shared memory with a tiny per-request lookup (hash+index). But that requires careful GC and memory quotas per tenant.
[04:47] Raj (Infra Eng): We're worried about memory pressure — our models + cache could saturate 80GB on A100. Any recommmended quantization to reduce working set?
[04:56] Nina (SE): Yes, quantization tradeoffs matter: FP16 halves activation footprint; INT8/4-bit can reduce weights dramatically but KV cache is primarily activations and keys which often remain FP16 for numerical stability. There's experimental 8-bit activations in some engines but it's model-dependent.
[05:12] Maya (ML Eng): We tried 4-bit weight-only quant and saw slight degradation on some QA tasks. Can Redwood do hybrid per-layer quantization?
[05:19] Nina (SE): We provide quantization recommendations per model: mixed precision (FP16 activations + 4-bit weights in FFNs) is common. We'll run evals against your held-out prompts.

--- Batching heuristics and SLOs ---
[05:33] Nina (SE): Batching: continuous batching is great for throughput, but it introduces queuing latency. We recommend adaptive batching: small immediate batches for p50 targets, and aggressive batching for background or high-throughput endpoints. Redwood runtime exposes per-route batching thresholds and max latency targets.
[05:52] Raj (Infra Eng): For a 50ms p95 SLO, what batch size ceiling do you recommend for our A100 nodes?
[05:59] Nina (SE): Roughly, for 8B models at 2k context, keep interactive route batches <= 6 to meet 50ms p95 on A100 FP16; TensorRT-LLM could push that to 8 in steady state but only after warmup and with reserved memory. We should benchmark with your exact tokenization.

--- vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM nitty gritty ---
[06:18] Nina (SE): Additional notes: TensorRT-LLM benefits from kernel fusion (lower launch overhead) and Tensor Cores for matrix work, but suffers if the model has many small ops or custom fused attention that the compiler can't fuse. vLLM is more flexible with custom ops and has mature KV handling, but you trade some absolute per-op speed.
[06:37] Maya (ML Eng): What about multi-GPU scaling? We plan NVLINK across two A100s.
[06:43] Nina (SE): Multi-GPU splits can be either pipeline or tensor-parallel. For NVLINK and tight latency, model sharding with synchronous RPCs introduces tail latencies. If your model fits single GPU with quantization, that's usually preferable for interactive SLOs. If not, the runtime can do synchronous pipelined stages but you'll lose a bit on p95.

--- Observability and traces ---
[07:05] Nina (SE): We'll share kernel timelines (per-stream) — note these sometimes show batched GEMMs as one large kernel with internal forks; labeling isn't perfect in traces. Also the Redwood Console can map token-level latency back to ops and show cache hit ratios.
[07:21] Raj (Infra Eng): Good, we need token-level breakdown in our monitoring.
[07:25] Alex (AE): We'll add that to the pilot scope.

--- Edge cases and failure modes ---
[07:33] Nina (SE): Failure modes: graph capture mismatch, CUDA OOMs on kernel fusion, and cache-thrash when many tenants evict keys simultaneously. For the latter, we recommend rate-limiting cache warmups and setting eviction thresholds.
[07:50] Ethan (DevOps): If we run Dedicated with burst capacity, do you have automated fallback to vLLM or CPU?
[07:58] Nina (SE): Yes — Redwood supports routing policies: primary TensorRT engines, with fallback to vLLM or smaller quantized variants when capacity is constrained. We'll show A/B policy configs.

--- Questions from KiteAnalytics ---
[08:12] Maya (ML Eng): Two quick questions: 1) can Redwood compile TensorRT-LLM engines with custom fused attention that we added? 2) any special driver versions to prefer?
[08:22] Nina (SE): 1) It depends — if custom ops can be represented as TRT plugins we can integrate; otherwise vLLM may be easier. 2) We recommend CUDA 12.x + cuBLAS/cuDNN matched to TRT version; we'll share the driver matrix.
[08:36] Raj (Infra Eng): Do we need to expose NVLINK as is, or will Redwood runtime treat each GPU as separate with RDMA?
[08:44] Nina (SE): For Private/on-prem you keep NVLINK; runtime can use it for fast cross-GPU transfers. We'll need low-level access during the pilot to validate topology.

--- Recap & next steps ---
[08:58] Alex (AE): Quick recap: Redwood to run TensorRT compile with your 8B model, share micro-benchmarks and CUDA traces; Kite to send prompt distribution and tail latency logs; both to meet for on-prem pilot planning week of 2025-07-21.

[09:25] Alex (AE): Will do. Anything else?

[09:36] Nina (SE): Yes, we'll include that in the initial runs.
[09:40] Alex (AE): Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and booking for the pilot kickoff.
